notes: Edition composed by Claude from the collected headlines, reading titles and metadata only.
Each narrative is an idea that joins several different events; what it joins is listed at the top. It commits to a claim, and the last rung of every narrative is the case against it. Read both.
Where a narrative continues one from the previous edition it says what has changed since; every edition is kept, so the reader can step back to where we were.

Each narrative ends with 'How we got here': four horizons, since 2020, since 2008, since 1989 and since 1945, each the start of a regime the headlines are living inside, and sometimes a fifth that reaches further back and names its own starting year. They are a trajectory, not a verdict.
The connections are made by the model, not by the publishers. Follow any headline to the original report before repeating it.
Books and trajectories appear only where they change how a fragment or a horizon reads.

readings.line: The Iran war's price rise holds central bank rates up, and households meet it as the highest mortgage rates in over a decade.
readings.change: The previous edition followed the war's fuel prices into air fares, luggage fees, asphalt and subsidies. Today the same price rise appears one step further on, in central bank decisions and in mortgage and loan rates in South Korea, Japan and Russia. The fuel headlines have not gone away, but the new evidence is about the cost of borrowing.
readings.claim: The Fed holds rates while its chair Warsh is asked about further hikes, the ECB is expected to hold, South Korean mortgage rates reach their highest in over 13 years, Hiroshima borrowers switch to fixed loans, Russia's central bank restricts long car loans, and the UK cuts its growth forecast over the Iran war. These are the same price rise seen at different points: fuel and food costs keep central banks from cutting, and lenders pass that decision on to households. The war that raised fares and asphalt prices in the previous edition is now being paid for in loan contracts that run for years.

events.label: Fed holds, Warsh weighs further hikes
ECB expected to hold its rate
Korean mortgage rates hit 14-year high
Hiroshima borrowers refinance to fixed rates
Russia restricts long-term car loans
UK growth cut, Australian inflation rises

rungs.label: Rate decisions in Washington and Frankfurt

fragments.label: The Fed holds
fragments.text: Business Day in South Africa reports that the Fed held rates 'as inflation risks persist', and Ideastream in the US that it held 'even as inflation remains stubborn'. Yicai in China reports Fed chair Warsh being asked whether further rate hikes may be needed. The question in these reports is whether rates rise again, not when cuts resume.

fragments.label: The ECB holds
fragments.text: Yle in Finland reports that the European Central Bank is expected to keep its policy rate unchanged. The headline gives no reason. A hold in the same week as the Fed's leaves borrowing costs in both currency areas where they are.

rungs.label: Borrowers in Korea, Japan and Russia

fragments.label: Korean mortgages
fragments.text: Hankyoreh reports that bank mortgage rates in September reached 4.88 per cent, the highest in 14 years and 5 months. Financial News reports fixed-rate mortgage loans entering 5 per cent for the first time in 13 years. Newspim reports a government debt-counselling hotline, 1375, opening on the 29th.

fragments.label: Hiroshima and Moscow
fragments.text: 47NEWS reports rising mortgage rates in Japan and borrowers in Hiroshima refinancing from variable to fixed rates. Izvestia reports that Russia's Central Bank will restrict long-term car loans from 2027. Both are responses to credit that is expected to stay expensive.

rungs.label: From fuel prices to loan rates

fragments.label: The chain
fragments.text: This Is Oxfordshire reports the UK growth forecast cut for next year 'amid Iran war impact', and the Sydney Morning Herald's live page reports Labor under pressure after an inflation rise. These sit in the middle of a chain: the war raises fuel and food prices, central banks hold rather than cut, and lenders pass the held rate to households. The previous edition followed the first link into fares and asphalt; the Korean and Japanese loan figures are the last link.

fragments.label: Fixed rates as a forecast
fragments.text: A borrower who switches from a variable to a fixed rate, as in Hiroshima, or a bank that prices fixed loans above 5 per cent, as in Korea, is betting that rates will stay high for years. Those bets turn a price shock into a cost carried for the length of a mortgage. The Russian car loan rule shows a central bank adding a limit on loan terms when the rate alone does not slow borrowing.

fragments.label: Separate causes
fragments.text: Japan's rates have been rising since the Bank of Japan ended negative rates in March 2024, for reasons in its own wage and price cycle. Korea's mortgage rates depend heavily on its housing market and household debt. Russia's car loan limit belongs to a war economy shaped by Ukraine and sanctions. None of the central bank headlines names Iran; only the UK growth forecast does.

fragments.label: What the events do not share
fragments.text: The events do not share an instrument: one is a policy hold, one a market mortgage rate, one a household's refinancing choice, one a cap on loan terms. They share only the direction of borrowing costs. A reader could explain that direction without the war at all, as inflation left over from 2022.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: The years since 2020 put two price shocks back to back. Supply disruption after the pandemic and the gas crisis after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 took US inflation to 9.1 per cent in June 2022. The Fed raised its rate from near zero to 5.25-5.5 per cent by July 2023, and the ECB moved its deposit rate up from minus 0.5 per cent. Cuts began in 2024 and were expected to continue. By these headlines, a war with Iran has since lifted fuel and food prices again: the UK growth forecast is cut 'amid Iran war impact', and the Fed under Warsh holds 'as inflation remains stubborn'. The Korean mortgage rate of 4.88 per cent is the household end of that sequence. The June 2025 strikes on Fordow were an earlier round of the conflict whose price effects now sit inside central bank statements. Whether today's inflation is driven by the war or is the remainder of the 2022 wave is contested.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: After Lehman Brothers failed in September 2008, the main central banks cut rates to zero and bought government bonds for most of a decade. The Fed held near zero from December 2008 to December 2015; the ECB went negative in 2014. Cheap money moved into housing. South Korean household debt rose to roughly the size of the whole economy, among the highest ratios in the world, and much of it carried variable rates tied to bank funding costs. That design is why a policy hold in Washington shows up quickly as a mortgage figure in Seoul, and why Korea is opening a debt-counselling line. Adam Tooze argues in Crashed that the 2008 rescue made the Fed the lender of last resort to the world's dollar system, which is why its decision is reported this morning from Johannesburg and Shanghai. A generation took loans assuming rates near zero; the Hiroshima switch from variable to fixed is that assumption being withdrawn.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: Japan's asset bubble burst in 1990, and the Bank of Japan spent most of the next thirty years at or below zero, cutting to zero in 1999 and going negative in 2016. Variable-rate home loans became the Japanese norm because the variable rate barely moved for a generation. The bank ended negative rates in March 2024, so the Hiroshima borrowers switching to fixed loans are reacting to the first sustained rise most of them have known. South Korea opened its capital markets in the 1990s and learned a different lesson in the 1997 crisis, when an IMF programme pushed interest rates above 20 per cent. Russia's central bank was created from the Soviet state bank in 1990 and has since used credit rules alongside rates; the limit on long car loans from 2027 is a rule of that kind. The three systems in this narrative came out of the 1990s with different memories of what a rate rise does to borrowers.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: The order built after 1945 tied currencies to the dollar, and the dollar to gold until 1971, so that a Federal Reserve decision became the reference for every other central bank. The 1973 oil embargo showed how a war in the Middle East becomes a price rise in every economy that imports fuel. The inflation of the 1970s ended only after Paul Volcker took the Fed rate close to 20 per cent in 1980 and 1981, and central banks since have been judged mainly on whether they let an oil price rise turn into general inflation. That is the test the Fed and the ECB are reported as facing this week, and the reason British and Australian headlines link war, prices and the next rate decision. Daniel Yergin's history of oil describes how a fuel became the organising price of the century. Whether 2026 resembles 1973 or the short oil spike of 1990 is not yet settled by these headlines.

readings.line: The AI data centre lifts profits at Asian hardware makers and has become a planning and security dispute in Europe.
readings.claim: Samsung's battery and IT units and Taiwan's CHPT report sharply higher profits on AI data centre demand, while Norway's parliament considers an urgent freeze on data centres, a Finnish city faces a police report for clearing forest for one, and Cloud.ru plans reserve capacity as Russian data centres come under attack. The same kind of building appears as a source of profit, a claim on land and power, and a military target. The profits in Korea and Taiwan and the objections in the Nordic countries are two ends of one expansion, and the costs are raised where the buildings stand rather than where the computing is sold.

events.label: AI data centre demand lifts Samsung results
Taiwanese test-equipment maker doubles profit
Norway proposes urgent data centre freeze
Finnish forest cleared for data centre
Russian data centres under attack

fragments.label: Samsung
fragments.text: Herald Economy reports a Samsung SDI third-quarter operating profit of 407.8 billion won, the highest in 12 quarters, on an 'AI data center boost'. Yle in Finland reports that the AI boom propelled Samsung's results, and Newspim that Samsung SDS's logistics business grew along with cloud. All three name computing demand as the source.

fragments.label: A Taiwanese supplier
fragments.text: Storm Media reports that CHPT's third-quarter profit doubled on strong demand for AI testing, with record earnings per share of 16.75 yuan and revenue expected to grow nearly 50 per cent next year. A second report has it in talks with more than five vendors on test interfaces for co-packaged optics, a component of data centre networks.

rungs.label: Objections in Norway, Finland and Russia

fragments.label: Freeze and forest
fragments.text: NRK reports an urgent proposal in Norway for a freeze on data centres. Svenska Yle reports that Villmanstrand, Lappeenranta in Finnish, cleared forest for a data centre and that a nature conservation district is preparing a police report. Neither headline mentions AI; both treat the building as a use of land.

fragments.label: A target
fragments.text: Kommersant reports that Cloud.ru is planning reserve capacity 'amid attacks on Russian data centres'. In Russia the data centre is now discussed as refineries and power stations are, as something a wartime opponent strikes.

fragments.label: The same object
fragments.text: Across these headlines the same kind of building is an earnings line in Korea and Taiwan, a claim on land and electricity in Norway and Finland, and a military target in Russia. The common factor is scale. A computing site large enough to move a battery maker's quarter is also large enough to need a parliament's attention and to be worth attacking.

fragments.label: Why the Nordic countries
fragments.text: Builders go north for cheap hydro and wind power, cool air and stable grids, which is why the disputes arise in Norway and Finland rather than in the countries buying the computing. The Norwegian proposal is a national response to a local cost: electricity and land used by servers are not available to households or other industry. The Finnish complaint is about forest, the oldest kind of land dispute.

fragments.label: Different buildings, different reasons
fragments.text: Samsung SDI makes batteries, and its data centre gain may come from energy storage sold to data centres rather than from computing. The Norwegian freeze may be aimed at crypto-mining sites, which Norway has debated restricting, rather than at AI. The Russian attacks belong to the war with Ukraine and would fall on any infrastructure. What the events do not share is a reason: one is a supplier's order book, one a nature complaint, one a drone campaign.

fragments.label: A Nordic sample
fragments.text: The objections come only from Nordic and Russian outlets in this collection. Disputes in Ireland, the Netherlands, the US or Malaysia, if any were reported today, are not in the sample. The split between Asian profit and European objection may reflect which newspapers were read.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: ChatGPT, released in November 2022, reached a hundred million users in two months and turned AI from a research field into a market for computing. The buildings that supply that computing need chips, batteries, cooling and large, steady electricity connections. By these headlines, the market now shows in Korean and Taiwanese results: Samsung SDI's operating profit at a twelve-quarter high on data centre demand, and CHPT expecting revenue to grow nearly 50 per cent next year on AI testing. The same years brought European energy prices to record levels after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which made Nordic hydro and wind power, cool air and stable grids more attractive to builders. The Norwegian freeze proposal and the Lappeenranta forest complaint are what that attraction looks like locally. In Russia the war has added a third role: Cloud.ru plans reserve capacity because data centres are now among the targets of drone attacks.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: After 2008, with interest rates near zero, investors funded companies that rented computing rather than sold it. Amazon Web Services, launched in 2006, grew into the largest business of its kind, Microsoft and Google followed, and the large data centre became the physical form of the platform economy. Shoshana Zuboff describes the business model those buildings served in the 2010s, the collection of behaviour as data. The Nordic countries entered early: Google bought a former paper mill at Hamina in Finland in 2009, and Facebook opened a data centre at Luleå in northern Sweden in 2013. Cheap electricity and tax terms drew them, and local opposition was small while the sites were few. Samsung SDS's cloud growth in this edition and the Finnish nature district's police report are the commercial and local ends of the same expansion, which reached its present size only when AI multiplied the demand for computing.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: The internet opened to commercial use in the early 1990s, and the Netscape listing of August 1995 was the first time the market priced it. The dot-com crash of March 2000 showed that the price could run years ahead of revenue. In the same decade South Korea and Taiwan built their electronics industries on supplying the hardware. Samsung became the largest memory maker in the world, and Taiwan's semiconductor cluster, centred on TSMC, founded in 1987, grew a ring of testing and packaging suppliers of the kind CHPT belongs to. Those firms earn from each wave of building, whichever software company wins. Their results this week rise on data centre orders as they rose on personal computers in the 1990s and smartphones after 2007. Whether the AI wave ends like 2000 or continues is the open question behind both the profits and the investment that funds the buildings.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: For most of the period since 1945 computing was a state project. The first large computers served weapons work and code-breaking; the field of artificial intelligence was named at a Dartmouth workshop in 1956; after Sputnik in 1957 the United States founded ARPA, whose network became the internet. Electricity grids were also built by states as national projects, Norway's hydropower among them. David Edgerton argues that what matters about a technology is the use and upkeep of its physical plant rather than the moment of invention. The data centre fits: the disputes in Norway and Finland concern land, electricity and forest, the oldest questions of infrastructure, now raised by private builders rather than ministries. The Russian attacks fit the older pattern too. Whatever a state comes to depend on becomes a military target, as railways, power stations and refineries did before, and Cloud.ru's reserve plan is a wartime precaution of a familiar kind.

readings.line: Former heads of government face courts at home, and their allies answer with amnesty bills, new laws and foreign refuge.
readings.claim: South Korea's special counsel again seeks, and by one report wins, a death sentence for former president Yoon Suk Yeol, while in Brazil Alcolumbre plans a pardon or amnesty for Jair Bolsonaro and Flávio Bolsonaro reaches the United States with Trump's consent; the same day an expert report contradicts Spain's Zapatero, India seizes Azam Khan's university and Indonesia's parliament opens its anti-corruption law to revision. In each, a former office-holder's case has reached the stage where it is settled either by a court or by politics. Korea is letting the court finish; in Brazil the routes out run through the legislature and a foreign host.

events.label: Yoon Suk Yeol faces second death sentence
Alcolumbre plans Bolsonaro pardon or amnesty
Flávio Bolsonaro leaves Brazil for US
Expert report contradicts Zapatero on jewels
Indonesia opens anti-corruption law to revision
India seizes Azam Khan's university

rungs.label: A second death sentence in Seoul

fragments.label: The Yoon case
fragments.text: Financial News reports that Yoon Suk Yeol, 'ringleader of insurrection', was again sentenced to death in his second trial and that Kim Yong-hyun received life imprisonment. Hankyoreh reports the special counsel seeking the death sentence. China's nbd.com.cn and Taiwan's ETtoday carry the case as a prosecution request, so the headlines differ on whether the court has already ruled.

fragments.label: The Bolsonaros
fragments.text: Tribuna do Norte reports that Alcolumbre plans a pardon or amnesty for Jair Bolsonaro. DW reports that Brazil cancelled the passport of Flávio Bolsonaro, who may have fled; El Colombiano that he passed through Ecuador, according to Argentine authorities; La Tercera that Trump confirmed he let Flávio and his family into the US because they 'were treated very unfairly'. Flávio's own version, in Tribuna do Norte, is that he 'left through Brazil'.

fragments.label: Spain, Indonesia, India
fragments.text: El Mundo reports an expert report contradicting Zapatero's account of a set of jewels, finding it unlikely they were made in the Middle East or before 2007. Merdeka reports the DPR's Commission III opening the option of revising Indonesia's Anti-Corruption Law after a proposal from Luhut. Punjab Kesari reports the Enforcement Directorate seizing Jauhar University, worth 1,170 crore rupees, in a money-laundering case against Azam Khan.

fragments.label: Court, legislature, host, statute
fragments.text: Set side by side, these cases show the routes open once a former office-holder is pursued. In Korea the court carries the case to a sentence. In Brazil allies in Congress prepare an amnesty and a foreign president provides entry. In Indonesia the law under which such cases are brought is itself opened for revision. Spain and India show an earlier stage, an expert report and an asset seizure, before any route is chosen.

fragments.label: Why the foreign host matters
fragments.text: Trump's admission of the Bolsonaro family turns a Brazilian prosecution into a matter between states, the reverse of Pinochet's arrest in London in 1998, when a foreign country held a former ruler rather than sheltered one. A former leader whose family can leave, or whose allies can legislate, is not in Yoon's position. The outcome depends on who holds the legislature and who will receive the accused as much as on the evidence.

fragments.label: Not the same offence
fragments.text: Yoon is tried over a declaration of martial law; the Bolsonaro amnesty concerns a conviction for a coup plot; Zapatero's jewels are a question of gifts and provenance; Azam Khan's case is money laundering by a state politician, which his party may call political targeting by the national government. Indonesia's revision may concern the commission's procedures rather than any person. What the events do not share is the act being judged: two concern seizures of power, the rest money.

fragments.label: An ordinary week
fragments.text: Former leaders and ministers are investigated somewhere every week. Korea and Brazil happen to reach decisive stages on the same day, and the Spanish, Indian and Indonesian items may be the normal background of corruption reporting gathered into a pattern by the coincidence.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: The decade's model of a contested handover was set on 6 January 2021 in Washington and repeated in Brasília on 8 January 2023, when supporters of Jair Bolsonaro stormed the three branches of government a week after Lula's inauguration. Brazil's supreme court later tried Bolsonaro for the coup plot and convicted him in September 2025. South Korea's case began on 3 December 2024, when President Yoon Suk Yeol declared martial law for about six hours; parliament overturned it and impeached him, and the special counsel charged him as ringleader of an insurrection, the charge in today's second trial. The decade's other answer also came from Washington: the January 2025 pardons of those convicted over the Capitol attack made a mass pardon an ordinary political tool. Alcolumbre's reported plan for Bolsonaro and Trump's admission of Flávio Bolsonaro's family draw on that precedent, while Korea follows the path of prosecution to sentence.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: The years after 2008 brought a wave of corruption prosecutions of sitting and former leaders. In Brazil the Lava Jato investigation, begun in 2014, jailed Lula in 2018 before the supreme court annulled his convictions in 2021; the reversal taught both sides of Brazilian politics to describe prosecution of their own leaders as persecution, the language of Trump's 'treated very unfairly'. In South Korea Park Geun-hye was impeached in 2017 and jailed, then pardoned in December 2021, continuing a Korean pattern of punishment followed by release. Indonesia's anti-corruption commission was weakened by a 2019 revision of its law, and the DPR's openness to a further revision after Luhut's proposal continues that argument. India's Enforcement Directorate has multiplied money-laundering cases against opposition politicians since 2014, the Azam Khan seizure among them. Levitsky and Ziblatt describe the risk of this period as courts used by whichever side controls them.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: The end of the Cold War made it possible to try former rulers without risking a coup. South Korea sentenced Chun Doo-hwan to death and Roh Tae-woo to prison in 1996 for the 1979 coup and the Gwangju killings; both were pardoned in December 1997. That sequence, a death sentence and then a political release, is the precedent over Yoon's case. In October 1998 Pinochet's arrest in London on a Spanish warrant showed a former ruler could be pursued abroad, and in 2002 the International Criminal Court opened. South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission offered a third way, amnesty in return for testimony. Brazil kept its 1979 amnesty law, which protected the military and was upheld by its supreme court in 2010, so Alcolumbre's plan revives an instrument Brazil has used before. Korea's courts, meanwhile, proceed on the model of 1996, and the question of a later pardon remains open.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: The Nuremberg trials of 1945 and 1946 established that the people who ran a state could be tried for what it did. For forty years the principle was applied mostly to defeated enemies. Many of the countries in this narrative were then governed by men who had taken power by force: Brazil's generals from 1964 to 1985, Park Chung-hee in Korea from 1961 until he was shot in 1979, Suharto in Indonesia from 1966 to 1998. Argentina's trial of its juntas in 1985 was the first time a state tried its own recent rulers in its own courts. Paul Ricoeur's question, what a society owes to the past it reopens and the past it closes, describes the choice between Yoon's prosecution and Bolsonaro's proposed pardon. The postwar order made trying a former ruler possible in principle; whether it happens has depended since on who controls the courts and the legislature when the ruler falls.

readings.line: Backup systems meant to catch human error failed on railways and grids this week, and official blame still starts with the operator.
readings.claim: A Spanish high-speed collision near Urda followed at least 15 warnings about faulty signalling, a Japanese JR train overran a station when its driver was drowsy and its automatic system did not activate, Bangladesh is investigating a grid failure and a three-hour outage of its identity server, Manila's airport has broken CCTVs, and Mexico lost internet services across several networks. In each, a layer meant to catch a failure was itself not working. The first official explanations, human error in Spain and drowsiness in Japan, point at the person rather than at the unmaintained system around them.

events.label: Urda collision after repeated signalling warnings
JR train overruns station, automatic braking fails
Bangladesh probes national grid failure
Bangladesh identity server down three hours
Broken CCTVs flagged at Manila airport
Internet outage across Mexican networks

fragments.label: Urda
fragments.text: El Comercio reports at least 15 InfoAdif warnings about signalling problems around Urda since 2024, and AVE drivers saying the signalling was already faulty at the site the day before. El País publishes the Atocha controller's instruction to the driver: 'Disconnect and reconnect, and resume at normal speed.' Franceinfo reports human error as the most likely cause.

fragments.label: Japan
fragments.text: Asahi Shimbun reports a JR train that passed through a station where it should have stopped, with braking 'delayed due to drowsiness', and that 'the automatic system also did not activate'. No injuries are reported. The account has the same two parts as Urda: a person who erred and an automatic layer that did not catch it.

fragments.label: Bangladesh
fragments.text: bdnews24 reports that the Power Division has formed a probe committee over a grid failure, and separately that the national identity server was 'down' for three hours, disrupting online services. Neither report gives a cause.

fragments.label: Manila and Mexico
fragments.text: Philstar reports broken CCTVs flagged at Manila's NAIA airport. Vanguardia reports an internet outage across Izzi, Totalplay, Telmex, X, ChatGPT, Fortnite and WhatsApp in Mexico. In both, a system treated as background stopped working.

fragments.label: Blame at the end of a chain
fragments.text: The Atocha instruction places a person between a signalling system already reported faulty and a train at speed. Calling the result human error names the last person in that chain and leaves out the fifteen warnings. El Comercio's report that this is the second fatal high-speed accident in ten months, shaking the campaign for the 29 November election, shows the argument moving from the driver's cab to the ministry. The Spanish Wikipedia's most-viewed pages included the earlier Adamuz and Santiago de Compostela accidents.

fragments.label: Upkeep as the shared factor
fragments.text: The Spanish, Japanese, Bangladeshi and Philippine cases share a protective layer that existed on paper and was not working on the day: signalling, automatic braking, a grid, cameras. These are failures of upkeep rather than of design. They come to light only when the primary system, a driver or a power plant, also fails.

fragments.label: Unequal events
fragments.text: The Urda collision killed 68 people, as other headlines in the collection report; the JR overrun hurt no one reported; the Bangladesh, Mexico and Manila cases are outages and defects with no stated harm and no stated cause. The Mexican outage may be a single network fault or an attack, and the Bangladesh grid failure may come from weather or demand. What the events do not share is consequence or cause: one is a disaster, one a near miss, the rest disruptions whose origin is unknown.

fragments.label: One crash shapes the sample
fragments.text: Half the evidence is Spanish. On a day without a major crash, the other items would read as routine outages of the kind found in any day's news, and no one would group them. The pattern may be the Spanish story lending its shape to unrelated reports.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: Since 2020 several of the networks in this narrative have been asked to carry more. Spain opened its high-speed lines to competing operators: Ouigo began running on the Madrid-Barcelona line in May 2021 and Iryo in November 2022, alongside Renfe, so more trains now use tracks and signalling managed by the state company Adif. Bangladesh suffered a nationwide grid failure in October 2022 that left most of the country without power for hours, and today's probe committee follows that precedent. Identity systems, airport cameras and consumer internet services have become things daily life cannot do without, which turns a three-hour outage of Bangladesh's identity server into national news. By these headlines the Urda collision is Spain's second fatal high-speed accident in ten months, and El Comercio's count of fifteen signalling warnings since 2024 suggests the maintenance record did not keep pace with the traffic. Whether that holds will be argued in the 29 November campaign.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: After 2008 Spain's public investment fell sharply as governments cut spending during the euro crisis, while the high-speed network kept growing until it was the longest in Europe. In July 2013 an Alvia train derailed at Angrois near Santiago de Compostela, killing 80. The first account blamed the driver, who was on a phone call and took a curve at more than twice the limit. The trial that ended in 2024 convicted both the driver and Adif's former head of traffic safety, because the curve lacked automatic speed protection. That case is the template for the Urda argument: franceinfo reports human error as the likely cause, El País publishes the controller's instruction, and El Comercio counts the warnings. The Spanish Wikipedia's most-viewed pages on 28 October included the Santiago and Adamuz accidents, which suggests readers were making the same comparison.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: Japanese National Railways was split and privatised in 1987, and the new JR companies ran dense timetables under commercial pressure. In April 2005 a JR West train derailed at Amagasaki, killing 106 passengers and the driver. The inquiry found the driver had been speeding to recover a delay of about ninety seconds, under a company regime that punished lateness with retraining, and that the curve lacked a modern automatic train stop. The Asahi report that a JR driver's braking was 'delayed due to drowsiness' and that 'the automatic system also did not activate' has the same two parts. Spain opened its first high-speed line, Madrid to Seville, in 1992, and reorganised its railways under European rules in the 2000s, separating track from trains. In both countries the 1990s turned rail into a business with performance targets, and after each accident the question became whether the person or the company had failed.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: Postwar states built national grids, railways and later data networks as public works, and added automatic safety layers after each disaster. Japan fitted automatic train stop equipment across its network after the Mikawashima collision of 1962, which killed 160. Ulrich Beck argued in 1986 that modern societies produce risks faster than they can assign responsibility for them, so that the argument over blame becomes the main politics of an accident. David Edgerton points out that most of a technology's life is maintenance, which is seldom news until it fails. The broken CCTVs at Manila's airport, the grid failure under investigation in Bangladesh and the signalling faults reported before Urda are maintenance stories that became news only when something stopped. The public bodies founded after 1945 still own or regulate most of these networks, which is why each failure ends in a probe committee or a minister's statement.
